title: Buy Now, Pay Later Is Trapping Millions of Americans
summary: Deep-dive video using Fed and CFPB survey data to show how loan stacking, demographic disparities, and invisible debt make BNPL risky.

assertions.quote: 63% of users have held multiple loans at the same time, and a quarter have juggled three or more
among black adults, it was 29% and among Hispanic adults, 26 against 12% of white adults

verdicts.note: Federal Reserve survey data shows this disparity, though it rests on a single underlying data source repeated across several videos.
Fed SHED: Black and Hispanic adults are more than twice as likely to use BNPL as White or Asian adults, and sizeable differences remain even after controlling for income and age.

FEDS Notes: Black and Hispanic women's BNPL use is more than double White (11%) and Asian (8%) women's; controlling for age, income and credit score explains only about half the Black-women gap and a quarter of the Hispanic-women gap, so most of the race-based gap persists.

assertions.quote: among users earning under $25,000, 40% paid late. Among users earning over $100,000, it was 11

verdicts.note: Federal Reserve survey data shows late-payment rates several times higher among lower-income users than higher-income users.
Fed SHED table 41: among BNPL users, the late-payment rate is 40% for incomes under $25,000 versus 11% for incomes of $100,000 or more.

assertions.quote: 11% of all users had one of these payments trigger an overdraft or insufficient funds fee from their own bank

verdicts.note: Federal Reserve survey data found roughly 1 in 9 users had a buy now pay later payment trigger an overdraft or NSF fee.

Fed SHED: since most BNPL users must enroll in autopay, 11% of all BNPL users had a payment trigger an overdraft or NSF fee in the prior year; among those charged extra for being late, 38% had an overdraft/NSF fee.
KC Fed: even with auto-repayments set up, BNPL users can incur overdraft or NSF fees from their bank if they lack sufficient funds to cover the auto-debit.

CFPB: not allowing borrowers to easily remove their autopay payment method 'could inadvertently lead to overdraft,' and lenders' repeated re-presentment of failed payments (up to eight times per installment) exposes consumers to further bank fees.

assertions.quote: most providers weren't reporting, and even where loans were reported, they didn't factor into scores
there is no statement, no balance, and nothing that adds it up for you

verdicts.note: This fragmentation is well documented in Federal Reserve and CFPB research as a structural feature of the pay-in-four market.

Because lenders do not typically report BNPL loans to nationwide consumer reporting companies, CFPB says data on multi-loan borrowers and total consumer debt is limited; 33% of borrowers held loans from multiple lenders in 2022.

KC Fed: because BNPL providers typically don't share customers' credit limits with bureaus or other BNPL providers, a user's summed credit limit across providers could exceed their ability to repay, and no single lender sees the total.

CFPB: because most BNPL lenders only make 'soft' credit inquiries and historically haven't furnished loan data to the bureaus, 'even with credit checking, lenders (BNPL or other lenders) have no lens into how much BNPL debt borrowers are carrying' across other apps.

assertions.quote: total outstanding pay in four debt in America sits around $3 billion against 1.23 trillion in credit card debt
